I have now completely rewritten this review, as my thoughts have developed more, and I want to do this review justice considering its popularity.
This is a 8/10, and in my top 10 favorite games of all time, BUT: [h1]I'm going to actually tell you if you'll like this game or not, BECAUSE IT IS NOT FOR EVERYONE[/h1] Though people preach a lot, this game's flaws can only be tolerated by the target audience. You are no less impressive if the game isn't for you. I had a friend get the DLC and ditch it after a while because he found it boring.

To enjoy this game you must be fine with these things:

- Dying to things completely outside your control: This can really piss people off, as you can die and have to redo entire sections due to complete jank-

(When I use this word, "Jank" I mean: Unnatural, and the feeling of being glitchy or strange. You already knew this, and would be able to figure it out from context clues, but some guy thought you were stupid and don't understand basic lingo. So there's the clarification you clearly needed).

It's part of the fun for a lot of people, it does really make you feel helpless, and like you're at the bottom of the foodchain, but some people really won't be able to appreciate it, which is totally fine.

- Repetitive elements: This especially applies to the DLC. Once you've seen all the areas, they don't (usually) change a ton from playthrough to playthrough. Your first run through the game will definitely be your longest by quite the margin.

- Survival Elements: This is not a platformer at its core. Survival elements can make this game quite tedious at times, and if you just want to run run run run all the time, you're going to be disappointed.

Purposefully jank mechanics. Rain World has one of the most janky and weird movement systems on purpose, and that can justifiably be frustrating to people. Even the combat is weird. You're mostly one shot to almost everything, and the combat involves finding spears, finding rocks, and throwing things at your enemies' weakpoints until they die. You don't get your spears back, you have to either find a new one or pull it back out of enemies, this is a type of combat I hadn't really seen before.

Play survivor first, it's the most liberating one to beat, and hunter is a different type of game pretty much.
The difficulty in this game is so unique though that I wouldn't blame you if you went Monk (the easy version).
Doesn't matter if you're one of the best Doom players in the world, this game's difficulty is WEIRD and out of the box. I'm the type of person to 100% games, nohit bosses, install mods to make the game harder, but I was not ready for the pure jank difficulty of this game.

I went on here in previous reviews talking about where I'd place it on my games ranking. After thinking about it for a while, I think it's moreso at around 6th place currently. Anyway, it's absolutely beautiful, the AI is jawdropping, the environments are fantastic, and even though I had no idea what was happening, the ending was rewarding to me (no Outer Wilds, but it was a good ending).

Having invested slighty more than 40 hours in Rain world at the time of this passage, I come to you, the public, at this late hour to deliver a most urgent plea.

I was once of a mind to decry the game for its unceasing brutality and unforgiving, unrelenting, unfair cycle of desperate survival and unforseeable death. Though I recognized its unique beauty and loved its dynamic, fluid, and yet cohesive mechanics, I was repulsed by its difficulty. I am in regret for this.

While I can't place blame on those who persist in disliking Rain World's foundational difficulty (I empathize with them, in fact: my first 20 hours were hell), I can offer a nugget of advice for those who would consider providing the game another opportunity: have patience, and learn of the world and your capability in it before establishing a "lifestyle" as the Slugcat.

My principle mistake when initially playing Rain World was permitting my expectations to override my actions. I occupied nearly 20 hours with practically no progress and an abundance of futility, and all because I was awaiting some firm directive which never came. In my frustration with this interminable cycle, I began to condemn certain aspects of the game, most notably the karma system. In time I became so desperate for some means of enjoying the game that I sought out a mod which rendered this scapegoat, the karma system, inconsequential. The result was... hollow. With nothing to penalize me, I was no longer obliged to inject purpose into my actions, and the game's value evaporated.

This was a moment of revelation for me. I realized that, in order to enjoy Rain World, I needed to seek its rewards and venture into its world and mysteries rather than flit axiously from one hibernation chamber to the next in perpetual fear of the consequences of curiosity. I needed to accept that this alien wilderness was harsh in excess, and that to survive it I must accomodate it and, at length, begin to predict it. I had been humbled to a slugcat and flung, directionless, into a world eager to swallow me. My sole guides were my intuition and ambition to explore, and my immersion in Rain World was contingent upon my willingness to exercise both. So I did.

My advice as a "veteran" is this: do not allow your fear of penalty to succeed your will to explore. Learn to live, not just survive, and perhaps you, too, will leave your heart in the hostile yet beautiful lands of Rain World.

[b] Rain or Pain? [/b]

Before making conclusion please read to the end. Within the entire playthrough and even after completing the game I've been hesitating on which review shall I write. For me that game was both - awesome and terrible. But once I forced myself to give it an answer - why, why do I want to write a negative review? Why do I partly consider this game as "terrible"? And you know what? There was only one reason - the PAIN. Yes, if I was developer I would've given it a beatiful "Pain World" name. With that being said, no matter how many people complain - [b]this game is HARD, and here's why: [/b] 

-there are no lives. Any mistake leads you to death. You need to practice a lot to become good enough to avoid being eaten by other predators
-every time you die, you lose karma. More karma you lose - more karma you have to gain again to pass through another location
-you have no idea of where locations are placed. The map is DRASTICALLY huge. There are so many places to visit and so many things to behold. However, there is an assistant who helps you get out by showing the way. But guess what? [spoiler]On my first playthrough I lost him and didn't even realize why[/spoiler]
-The game is hard even from its early stage of survival, but the thing is, the more you play - the harder it gets. You suffer by trying to find new place but once you reach it it only gets harder. There are new predators and the old ones can be met even in a higher quantity than before
-The shelters are not that easy to find unless you know the map. You can progress pretty good but at the end die by rain which is also a pain because you'll be losing karma and then... you'll have to restart it from the previous shelter without guarantee that you'll make it good this time again.

So the only thing I hated this game for was its hardcore. Also, I've started playing as a Survivor, not as a Monk. After completing the game I've heard that even Monk is not easy to play as so if you still think that you can easily manage this game on Survival Mode without having experience I'd recommend you to think properly. If you want to make it hard - start on Survivor. If you want to make it easier (but still i'm not sure if it's easy) - start as a Monk. 

Still, I'm not saying that being a hard game is disadvantage but I had to mention my pain. Now, about [b] good sides of this game. As for me, these have to be mentioned:[/b]

-amazing soundtrack. Can't say much about it - it's just something awesome and as everything else it's perfect for this style of game
-the unique and awesome art style. I can never say this game is "cheap-looking"
-the idea. I cannot say much about the story because it's more about idea. The world is awesome - the creatures are terrifying, the plot is unpredictable and special. It all makes game look unique, and it definitely is
-mechanics. Those are also unique in this game. They look simple, but trust me, there are way more moves which can be performed if you learn them. You can watch "Rain World advanced movements" videos, which might help you a lot. Sounds weird but the movements and environment in this game sometimes seemed more realistic than the real life, but of course it's just an expression and is described with details below
-the smartest entities I've ever seen in my life. And I'm not only mentioning virtual ones. They're actually smarter than some of my friends. The predators act completely like real - some hide and attack when you come closer; some follow you until you get out of vision, and then, find the best spot to track prey, or slowly keep following you by moving closer to shelter or pipe. Actually, you're not the only prey in this game. They are all fighting each other, and their movements... It all looks so cool, so real... I've never seen anything like it.
-The game can be replayed many times. There are things and "mobs" you can unlock, so you can play on arena (like sandbox), and there are some choices which you can accept during the playthrough. There are also different strategies which can be tried. I mean, you can build your own route, so you know where to go on earliest and latest stages of your run.

-------------‐-‐-------------------------------------------


One thing which I wanted to mention - if you have problems with orientation in space or really don't know what to do and where to go - you can google "full Rain World map". Choose the map which shows which locations are connected to which. Don't spoil what they include but still, you're not forced to make it too "hardcore" if you don't want it to be. Getting lost for many hours without making any progress while moving to the wrong direction may ruin your game experience. But again, it's mostly recommendation for people like me who struggle with map orientation.

Rain World is a 2D survival platformer where you're playing as the lowest of the food chain trying to survive a wildlife that has outlasted its cycle of life while making sense of a long lost world in ruin and your life in it.
It will not be easy.
You won't fully understand what you're doing at first.
You will get lost and die a lot by the most spine-chilling and cortisol-inducing creatures you have ever seen.
You WILL find it unfair.

And that's because it is, your odds at succeeding are really small. It's not a conventional game by any means, a lot of its story themes and game mechanics might seem cryptic at first, the control scheme is weird (but you get used to it after some time) and ennemies are moving in a kind of erratic and unpredictable way. I really like all of this to be honest, might be one of the only games out there that literally says "fuck it we ball" by design.

And yet, all of that is contrasted by the most beautifully crafted and heartbreakingly rich fictionnal universe in sync with the fantastic gems and colossal amounts of soundtracks, absolutely massive interconnected map, insane procedural animations, deep movement mechanics and item interaction systems, and pixel art visuals a game could ever have.

Rain World is simply put, my favorite game of all time.

At its core, it is disguised as a live action roleplaying nature documentary with lots of advanced tech for experienced players... But you will get better and get through it and when you start to peel its layers, you will realise that deep down, it is in fact about surviving loss, enduring hardships and friendships, what you can (or cannot) make of it and the beauty of it all.

I have basically done everything and anything this game, its DLCs (and its modding community) could ever offer and I still come back to it from time to time to immerse myself in its mysterious and beautiful world.

One thing I also get from other people is that: it is not a game for everyone, the journey from start to finish is exhiliratingly painful and even if you're the most tolerant gamer to ever exist, this game will make you ragequit more than once. But if you decide to stick with it just a bit longer, as you play, you might start to uncover its well hidden secrets waiting behind this thin veil for you to open. And once this happens, you will realise that it is an absolute one-of-a-kind gem of a masterpiece that everyone should at least experience once.

Absolutely phenomenal. I started the game, died a lot, got frustrated and wasn't sure when I'd enjoy it. I wanted the full experience but I was also struggling. I beat the first 'chapter' of the game but wanted to restart after having an awful time and resorted to cheating with the dev console to skip some levels.

Forum users helped me with encouragement, and also admitted that they themselves used mods and some of the accessibility settings in the remix option to ease into it.

I also learned more about the movement of the game; it's all a learning experience and while I won't spoil anything here I will say that you can outmaneuver a lot of predators with speed, agility or both.

Finally, I beat the game without strictly cheating (maybe some would account accessibility options as cheating, but I still beat the game using regular tools at my disposal)

Here's some settings / mods I'd suggest:

- Play as survivor instead of monk (Food might seem tough at first but don't worry, the experience IS better as survivor)
- Monk style gates (Once you enter an area, its unlocked permanently)
- DO NOT USE 'Disable karma requirements' (High karma gates are used to say 'this is a hard area'. I turned this off in my initial playthrough and it meant I went into a really hard area by accident and gave me a horrible experience).
- Loading screen tips (There's some VITAL information I never figured out, wish I turned this on sooner)
- Maximum rain timer (Normally its RNG how much time you get, but I just used this so that I always have forever before the rain. Turn off as you get better)
- Slug senses (ability to see a visual 'threat' meter so you know enemies are nearby)
- Breath time leniency (Makes it so that you don't die as quickly when out of oxygen under water)
- Sharpener mod (allows you to resize window)
- SBCameraScroll (Combines appropriate rooms into long rooms where the camera follows you, great to avoid BS deaths where something is pixels away from you but offscreen so you had no idea. Also helps you know which ways you can go)
- Infinite Spears (This is kind of cheating, but spears are very important. I turned this on at first so that I could get used to using spears in and out of combat as I was very bad with my throws and end up losing them. You can then turn down the number of spears so instead of having infinite spears on your back you just have more than one. Eventually turn this mod off when comfortable with using the spears around you)
- Some people like the health bar mod but I never used it

Good luck and let me tell you, it's worth it.

This. F**king. Game.

I can comfortably say that beating Rain World is one of my most prized accomplishments when it comes to gaming. Not only because it's very difficult in a refreshingly unique way - more on that later - but also because the [i]spiritual significance[/i] of the game, the ending in particular, left an ever-aching scar on my heart that refuses to heal even years later.

There's this general belief that game journalists suck at games; I don't want to get into that right now, but I honestly believe that Rain World simply blindsided a lot of its more mainstream reviewers with its unconventional control scheme and strange, dynamic difficulty. This isn't a 2D platformer. The slugcat cannot really jump like we're used to; instead, it has a handy set of other movement abilities, and learning them in spite of your instincts is required to get anywhere.

And this is on top of the other unusual design choices. The world is incredibly interconnected and if you're persistent enough, there's nothing really preventing you from doing stuff out of order and even skipping a lot of the game. No worries though - the chances of you doing that on accident are very low.

What really makes Rain World shine, however, is the way its difficulty works. Almost all hard games can be learned, and that's what you're expected to do. Learn the steps and execute the dance. But Rain World shuffles things up every time you die. Enemies appear in different locations. A route you took last time might be inaccessible this time around due to a bunch of lizards fighting for turf. Sure, you could try sneaking past. Or even fighting them. But as a general rule you're not a fighter; you have to use a mixture of trickery, stealth, being quick on your feet and occasional violence to get by.

In other words, you're squarely in the lower half of the food chain. Yes, there are creatures that are below you that you can hunt and consume, but most things want to make a snack of you instead. And they will. Oh yes, they will.

The most memorable and glorious moments of the game will be where you will have barely escaped with your life over and over again in a single cycle and miraculously managed to find shelter just before the rain came. And as you start to really understand the workings of the world and the abilities of your slugcat, moments such as those will come more and more often. That's its true power.

On top of all that, Rain World has a spiritual component - one that is not immediately clear, but as you keep playing, you'll begin the true significance of a lot of stuff. I don't think it's practical to completely unravel the plot by yourself due to the insane things you need to do to get some pieces of info, though; I had to consult the wiki to really understand. But it's fine - you'll still get a very satisfying and emotional experience if you go only with what you can find by yourself.

And above all else - it's a very, very unique game, even by indie standards. Difficult, yes. But possible to learn and to master. Complex. Obtuse, perhaps; but so incredibly satisfying. Not for everyone, for sure - and yet, I implore you to check it out. I'm incredibly grateful to the Universe that I did and refused to give up.

I would recommend Rain World and especially its expansion to anyone that likes platformers and post-apocalyptic vibes. However, the base game with the default settings has some major issues, resulting in the time you spend being angry & frustrated, questioning why you haven't un-installed the game already, being longer than the time you are excited & impressed, which is never good. To avoid these issues, do the following:

Install the “SBCameraScroll” mod from the Steam workshop. By default, the camera is not centred on your character, and instead jumps abruptly when you reach the current edge of the screen. If there is an enemy right past said edge, you won't be able to see them in time to react to their attack (and your character always dies in one hit). I can not emphasise enough how annoying it is to die this way, and this mods fixes the problem by adding a smoothly scrolling camera. As a bonus, it also creates a parallax effect in some areas, making them look even more impressive.

Also install the “No Expedition Permadeath” mod, if you wish the play the expeditions game-mode (which is lots of fun). There is a lot of RNG in the game, which often leads to your death, especially for new players. If you can immediately continue playing from the last checkpoint, such RNG is a source of laughs, but if you instead lose 30 minutes / an hour / three hours of progress this way, you might never play the game again. Do yourself a favour and get rid of permadeath with this mod. For the same reason, if you wish to play the Hunter’s campaign (boring – play the DLC campaigns, expeditions, or challenges instead), you should set “Hunter Cycles” in the Remix tab to some high value, like 999.

Many improvements can be unlocked through the in-game Remix tab, which allows players a lot of customisation. Feel free to experiment with it, but the two settings I always enable are “Visual breath meter” (so you actually understand when you are drowning) and “Pull spears from walls” (aiming is challenging – this way you will get another chance to throw your spear by being able to recover it).

Lastly, read an online movement guide (all should be spoiler-free), as the game is awful at explaining even the basic movement controls. For example, when your character somehow enters a tunnel ass-first (which slows you down by a lot), you can press the jump key plus an arrow key to reorient yourself in the right direction.

I hope this review hasn’t put you off from the game, as Rain World really is quite special once you get the hang of it - it keeps on drawing me back even after hundreds of hours of gameplay.

My advice for new players would be to try to enjoy exploring and understand that deaths will happen, and that they are part of the experience, but almost 100% of the time they are avoidable, and you can learn how to avoid them through practice. If that isn't enough to enjoy the game though, playing with a friend who has already played it or having them watch to give you help can be really encouraging and teach you a lot about the game. Also, I would recommend maybe looking up a move-tech guide, as the game doesn't teach you most of the move-tech (and there is A LOT) and some of it is a little weird to learn but really fun once you do. Other than that though, I would HEAVILY recommend not looking up things like routes, playthroughs, or story because it can ruin some of the amazing experiences this game has to offer, but do whatever you want lol. I've seen a lot of people who dropped the game at first and then watched a playthrough of the game and came back to do it themselves, so if it's what you need, go ahead. Also, with Downpour, there is a ton of different campaigns to play, so spoiling one campaign doesn't ruin everything. I didn't expect this review to be this long lol, but hopefully it's useful for someone.

It’s common knowledge that good games are fair. Every failure should be the fault of the player, and any deviation from this standard makes for poor game design. This is the path of logic most games follow very closely, and to great effect. Gaming’s hall of fame is filled with titles that would be considered “fair” by most.

However, the necessity for fairness has some knock-on effects. It can make games feel samey and uninspired, and can even run the risk of breaking immersion. Games as a medium still have so much potential to evolve, so one could argue that fair gameplay doesn’t equate to good gameplay.

This raises an interesting question:

Do games have to be fair to be good? Sit and think on that for a second.

In my eyes, Rain World is proof that unfairness can be great. It’s a side scrolling open world sandbox that liberally borrows ideas from the survival genre but cuts out the fat. In short, Rain World is a portrayal of animalistic survival, rather than resource-gathering survival. In an era of tired, boring, and uninspired survival mechanics, Rain World feels dynamic and alive in a way most games don’t.

Surviving Rain World isn’t easy. Nature is cold, cruel, and unforgiving, a sentiment reflected best by the game’s rich ecosystem. Animals have complex behaviors, with easily identifiable traits and agendas of their own. Some will want a bite, and others won’t bat an eye at your presence.

The game uses a karma system to dictate progress through various zones. If you rest at a shelter with enough food to survive, your karma rank goes up. Meet an untimely death or quit mid-game, and that rank goes down. Exploring new areas requires a certain rank or higher, meaning that some areas force the player to live in their surroundings until they’ve proven their worth.

All this may seem incredibly daunting, and it should be. Rain World is genuinely unfair. If you are interested in purchasing this game, you shouldn’t have expected anything less of Mother Nature. Throughout my playthrough, I’d wager that around 1 in every 5 deaths was unavoidable. Your mileage may vary.

This is a game that will put you in a dark place if you aren’t careful, but there are positive qualities that shine through in times like this. Rain World is a bleak but beautiful place, with environments teeming with history and detail. The melancholic soundtrack, while sparse, accentuates the game’s drearily gorgeous environments perfectly. The dense ecosystem ebbs and flows with time, changing depending on the player’s actions. The final result is that Rain World is a place of extreme darkness, but yet… what a warm darkness it is.

Rain World is a game that isn’t going to be for everyone. That being said, there is a way to enjoy the game without its more difficult mechanics. Even so, I’d still suggest playing as “The Survivor” to get the best experience.

There’s something about surviving Rain World that is truly unlike any game I’ve ever played, and that is an experience only found once in a blue moon. In a survival genre devoid of ideas, Rain World stands tall as a game I’ll always come back to. Next time I’ll be sure to bring an umbrella.

This game is not half as hard as people say. It's only hard if you convince yourself you mustn't die under any circumstances. In reality, dying is no big deal.

You'll die a lot at first, but death is not permanent. Sure, there's a cost - you lose a level of karma, but recouping it is nothing. You gain a level of karma when you hibernate, and you only have a few levels to begin with. To hibernate you need to eat four pieces of food, but that's much easier to do than it sounds. You just have to find the bats' nesting grounds and where the blue bells grow and then you 're guaranteed a meal every day. 

If you can't get to your shelter before it starts raining, or if something grabs you, you die and respawn in the shelter, with one less level of karma.  That hardly even sets you back at all: karma is only used to unlock passage to new areas, and there is literally nothing forcing you to rush. Each area is huge, so there's plenty of time to explore and get to know all the nooks and crannies of one area, before you move on to the next. In theory, you are trying to be reunited with your family, but mechanically there is nothing in the game play forcing you to keep going- if you wanted you could stay put forever. And the more time you spend in each area the more you get to understand the world, and that makes it easier to survive longer.

The thing to keep in mind is that you're not Conan the Barbarian, you're a baby animal with a body like jell-o'. You can't fight very well, your only chance is to run and bolt into a hole. On the plus side, you're faster than the things that want to eat you and in any case you should be way smarter than them. 

Use your nugget. Feed before you go out exploring, not at the last moment before it rains. Keep an eye on the timer as you travel so you know how long it takes to traverse each part of the map and you don't risk straying too far from shelter. There is plenty of time to explore before the rain comes. And you should always eat as much as you can and always try to get to your hibernation shelter with your belly full, to make your life easier next day. You wouldn't even call all that resource management- it's just good sense.

Some reviews complain about the controls and the way the slugcat moves. Here's a little secret: if you learn the world's physics well you can move very fluidly and very, very fast. The only things that can move faster than you are the bats, and you can even surprise them with a sudden burst of speed or a well-timed jump. If you just push the jump button you don't jump too high, but if you press Pick Up at the end of a jump you can grab on to things even if they look slightly beyond your reach. You also get some special moves: you can coil up like a spring and jump three times your length, and you can do backflips to jump about twice your height. These take some practice, but, again, there's no need to rush, you can take your time.

If you've ever played Wipe Out, it's very similar: until you get a feel for the physics of moving around, you keep bumping into stuff and bouncing about and losing speed. But once you get the hang of it, and learn the lay of the land, you can really fly.

People compare this game to Dark Souls. It's nothing like Dark Souls. It's not even a fighting game. If you're looking for similar games, it's like Limbo, and Inside, and Abe's Odyssey. The "grind" in Rain World is like in those games: you have to solve a puzzle and you'll keep dying and retracing your steps until you get it right. Then you'll have to solve a new puzzle. And you'll be rewarded with knowing you conquered a beatiful, hostile world with just the power of your wits.

It's an absolute embarrassment for the entire video games "journalism" industry that this masterpiece received mixed to negative reviews, most of which cried petulantly about the difficulty level. This is one of the boldest, most ambitious, creative, ingenious and unique games ever made, a fully realised vision that deserves better than reviewers who straight up don't understand the point of given design decisions, the concept of ludic tone or atmosphere, or in some cases just didn't understand what a certain mechanic's point is. This should have been cherished and celebrated, but it's already a semi-obscure cult classic instead.

A lot of people try to say that this game is not for everyone, but I don't believe that either. This game IS for you as long as you're willing to rise to its level. Come on. Put the work in. It is punishing, it has a gruelling difficulty curve, but all that aside, Rain World is also thrilling, compelling and rewarding in a way that barely anything else can dream of achieving, and it's due to its own tough love that it succeeds at that. Suffering is part of the deeper message here, and it's so weird how the same people who were willing to talk down to us about how bloated "AAA" game of the exact second is "gaming's Citizen Kane moment" or that a walking simulator devoid of actual gameplay is some transgressive arthouse masterpiece we are obligated to recognise are unable to see the actual, real artistic vision on display here just because it isn't immediately gratifying to them. Utterly pathetic.

Also, the AI is basically the best I've ever seen, in any video game ever. This here should be studied in university level programming and game design courses. It needs to be picked apart and understood. Some of the behaviours on display here are nothing short of astonishing.

Rain World is not a metroidvania, it's not an action platformer; it's always been an *ecosystem simulator*. I'd recommend it to every biologist or naturalist or ecology enthusiast out there. If you mistake this game for what it's not, you'll be very frustrated - all your intentions will be dashed and you'll give it up quickly, but if you're willing to accept and learn from failure, you'll find a beautiful intricate experience like no other. You're a little lost animal in an unforgiving world. Endeavor as such. 

Take your time. Test out your environment. The gameplay loop is relatively simple - fill up on food, evade predators, find a safe place to sleep before bone-crushing rain pounds you to dust. When resources run out or you feel ready, trek to find the next gate and move on. 

ALWAYS CARRY A SPEAR. Eventually the wacky movement will become second nature, you'll move with confidence, death becomes but a mild inconvenience, because like sleep like death, you wake up again. Whether you want to or not. 

Good luck!

I’ll start with the details. The pixel art looks incredible. The sound design is great. It’s rare to see the full potential of procedural animation realized, but Rain World does it. Every part of this world looks and feels alive. The excellent AI of the game’s various inhabitants contributes to that as well.

The gameplay is a more complicated topic. That’s not a cop-out way of saying the game isn’t fun to play – it is. But it’s also infuriating. Death comes for you easily and often unfairly. It’s not a roguelike, but if you can’t stand roguelikes I would hesitate to recommend this game to you.

The controls are in a similar situation. They’re not bad, and there’s an incredible depth of skill that can be achieved with them – once you’re done exploring this game on your own, check out the wiki’s movement guides. I’ve come to enjoy the controls, but only after a great deal of frustration.

This frustration is a core part of Rain World. You could not tell the story that the developer is trying to tell, could not provide the profound experience that Rain World does, without this frustration.

All the same, I’d recommend to everyone that they enable the “Remix” plugin on the “Classic” preset immediately. The quality-of-life changes this gives are invaluable, and don’t diminish the experience in any way. The other options can be tried on a case-by-case basis.

The Downpour DLC is absolutely worth it, and enabling the “More Slugcats” plugin that it grants you access to right out of the gate will provide worthwhile additional content in all your playthroughs. You should start with Survivor, the white slugcat, regardless.

If you can stick with it through to the end, Rain World will absolutely be worth the time you put into it. 9/10.

Rain World is a masterpiece. I am not using this word lightly, this game has undoubtedly been a huge influence on my life.

Anyway, onto the game itself.
In Rain World, you play as a small animal - a wet and pathetic little otter thing called a slugcat - surviving in the ruins of an alien world. This is a world of derelict structures and burgeoning ecosystems, a world that is dead and yet so very alive. The line between ruin and nature is blurred into insignificance, as new life grows from a heap of decay. Rain World's beautiful pre-rendered environments convey the experience of a small, nimble animal extremely well. Cities are shown not through living spaces but basements, alleyways and storm drains. Pipes and rusted rebar scaffolds are not background objects but core geometry features of level design. Rain World thus has a wonderfully fresh take on ruined environments.

The gameplay itself is wonderfully unorthodox. While it takes some of the bare bones of a metroidvania, its progression is almost incomparable. The slugcat does not gather upgrades, and has every ability from the start. Instead, Rain World's progression is based on exploration and knowledge alone.

Rain World's story is one of the best I have ever seen. I can't really elaborate, as it's best experienced yourself. I could say a lot about it, but nothing that does it justice.

This game is a damn masterpiece. Don't you think that usually in video games, when an enemy is chasing you, the dev decides to make it so that the enemy is constantly stopping/slowing down mid chase to avoid frustrating the player? Well, Rain world says "fuck that, and fuck you" to the players.

Every enemy has its own extremely complex AI. They all have their unique behavior and personalities. All of them have the exact same goal as you: find food and survive. While your food is mostly bats and fruits, their food is you. So your job is to find food for yourself while avoiding becoming food to larger enemies. Sound simple enough, but you quickly realize how intelligent the AIs are. 

Smarter enemies can adapt to your action and find different ways to try eat you. Enemies can fight each other to fight for food, and they can attempt to eat another smaller creatures that isn't you. There is no scripted encounters in this game. Everything is purely the cause of the AIs interacting with each other. This has its downside of course, as it can create unfair scenarios and trap the players in insane situation, but that is the beauty of this game. 

The world is alive, and you are not the main character. You're just another creature in the world with an established food chain trying to survive. Other creatures can kill and be killed by you, their environment or other creatures. Big predators can be eaten by an even bigger predators, and you're just a tiny slugcat trying to survive in the midst of everything. 

This game is truly the most "alive" game I've ever played. Absolutely recommend.

One of the greatest, most powerful single player experiences I've ever pushed my way through. And I say pushed literally, it took several restarts, each one of my attempts lasting up to a couple of hours, before the game finally started to stick with me. If you have any interest in this game and its world, I beg you, do not spoil a moment of it for yourself. Do not look up a map, or walk-through of any kind. Go in completely blind. It will be worth the pain.

There are plenty of times in the game where it just won't be fun, and that's okay. Rain World is a living, breathing ecosystem that thrives all on its own, without any interference from you, the player. If you try to see the game as a 'move from A to B' kind of experience and push through to see the 'story', however much of it there may be, you will hate it. You really do have to put yourself in the little Slugcat's shoes, just trying to survive, not venturing far from your shelter, leaving for essential food and supplies before returning at the end of the day. Take a long, long while to learn the controls and how they work, push the limits of your mobility and simply watch the wildlife around you as you slowly piece together how it acts, what it hunts for, the things it runs from. You need to immerse yourself entirely in the experience of being the Slugcat, and live. It's a grim, oppressive environment, but there are so many moments of wordless, environmental storytelling, and interactions with other creatures that I will remember for the rest of my life. There truly is nothing like Rain World, and there never will be a game world of this scale or feeling ever again.

Progress comes from the expectation that the player "studies" the game through careful observation of the environment or just trial and error. The skill ceiling is ridiculously high and the process of learning Rain World's rules can at times be very difficult and requires you to experiment, die and backtrack a lot. Rain World's lore is one of grand scale: The story feels epic, ancient and tragic. This game is designed with so much detail, life and layered complexity that you can't help but be fascinated by it, and this desire to understand drives your urge to keep going and see what happens.

Rain World is pretty much a "hard simulation" of what survival in the real wilderness would feel like, taken to its rawest, most extreme form. It does an excellent job of selling this feeling of isolation, high-stakes danger and being just a tiny insignificant part of a much grander world. Overcoming its challenges and learning its secrets are rewarding on a deeply personal level that I haven't felt in any other game.

One of the best gaming experiences I've had. This game is definitely not for everyone, especially not people who: 
1. Are easily frustrated.
2. Are looking for fast-paced progression.

Pros:
A very beautiful art style
The soundtrack is great
The lore of the world is intriguing
It's TOUGH. Not just "hard" but actually really really tough. Most things kill you in a single hit, and you get punished rather severely for dying (explained in cons). Of course this won't be a pro for everyone, but it was for me.
Managing to get through a difficult area feels amazing every time.

Neutral:
Overall progression is slow-paced, though encounters with the flora and fauna can get extremely tense.
All movement is based on the physics engine which makes everything move around super smooth.
Since all movement is based on physics, you can expect to see some buggy/wonky movement of the creatures in the world (Including the character you play as).
There's barely anything telling you where to go, which can often make you feel lost.

Cons:
To be able to progress to new areas, you have to have a certain amount of karma. Every time you hibernate (or save) without dying, you get an extra karma point, which caps at 5. Though every time you die, you lose one. If you want to progress to another area but you don't have the right amount of karma, you sometimes end up having to hibernate in the same area 4 times in a row, which can get rather repetitive, though I never had huge problems with this myself, I can certainly see people struggling with this mechanic. (NOTE: They are adding a new character who does not need karma to progress to other areas)
It doesn't help that "cheap" deaths happen occasionally. (Getting instakilled by an enemy you couldnt see)

Though it is without doubts one of my favorite games on steam, it's not meant everyone.

This really does sound like the opening to a negative review, but I assure you it's not. You are just a feeble slugcat in a bustling yet abandoned ecosystem, slowly figuring out how to deal with predators, prey and the various tools at your disposal, littered across the land. You will learn things. Each thing you learn will give you a little advantage over the world and the creatures, and thus a means to survive another day. This is [b]exactly[/b] what an animal needs to do in an unfamiliar place. You and the slugcat are one and the same, and it is so very easy to get immersed in the game.

Rain World's visuals are phenomenal, the music adapts to the world around you, the world wraps around beautifully so it's a joy to explore, there is a 92-page document on the movement (almost none of which is explained to you) and learning/mastering new things is euphoric, and conquering each small feat of survival is oh so satisfying -- but Rain World is hard. It's unforgiving. The world goes on with or without you and you are most definitely on the bottom half of the food chain. Small, insignificant. Because of the unscripted nature of the game, some deaths and shortcomings are simply not avoidable. Especially for those who are new to the game. To truly enjoy Rain World, you need to have patience and perseverance. If you have these things, you're going to have an experience you won't soon forget. If you don't, you'll be frustrated to no end and wind up hating the game.

Definitely worth full price for this one. Rain World combines with Outer Wilds and Slime Rancher to make my top 3 games. I can't wait to see what's in store for the DLC, and I have no doubt that it will make me love this game even more.

Edit: Downpour is amazing. Outer Wilds is still my favourite game for sake of emotional significance, but Downpour is a very compelling argument.

I bought this game expecting to be the main character.

Turns out I'm a protein bar.

Rain World is what happens when a nature documentary gains sentience and decides you personally deserve to lose. Every creature has hopes, dreams, ambitions, and an overwhelming desire to make sure you never reach the next shelter.

The game doesn't hold your hand. It doesn't even acknowledge you have hands.

Every time I thought I understood the ecosystem, the ecosystem laughed, spawned three new lizards, and introduced me to a bird the size of a small apartment.

The AI is genuinely incredible. Half the time predators are hunting each other. The other half they've formed a temporary committee dedicated to making my day worse.

Movement starts out feeling like you're controlling an overcaffeinated wet sock. Twenty hours later you're chaining backflips, spear throws, wall jumps, and pipe tech like you've been training under a slugcat sensei your whole life.

The rain itself deserves an Oscar. Nothing motivates efficient route planning quite like hearing the sky announce, "Your survival subscription has expired."

This game somehow makes finding a tiny hole to sleep in feel like defeating the final boss. Every successful cycle has the emotional payoff of paying off your mortgage.

Would I recommend it?

Absolutely.

Would I recommend it to my friends?

Only the ones I'm willing to lose.

This game's ai is strikingly advanced. Creatures in this game are strategic, some critters even keep track of your actions, which affects your reputation with that species, similarly to crows. You may even tame some beasts, though this can take a long time. For example, some creatures may be protective of their family, and act with hostility when you threaten one of their kind, while others may rely on audio cues to locate their prey, and cannot see you crawl past them. Some creatures may even fight with their own species, allowing you to escape while they're occupied. You can tell the history of a certain species based on appearance, items, and special interactions. The ecosystem feels so real and alive, and the creature ai does an amazing job at immersing you. 

Some problems require advanced solutions. What seems like an uncrossable gap or an unclimbable wall can be overcome by using the various items and creatures in the area. You may even learn some new movement techs along the way, and progress even further. If you cannot figure something out, it is not wrong to look things up. This game is strikingly complex, with many easy-to-miss attributes. If you're not the kind of person that interacts with everything they can, then it might be right to grab your phone and have the wiki on standby.

This game is primarily exploration as well as survival, you will need to progress by getting to new areas and going through a rather linear path. Though, if you want to take the scenic route and find every possible area, you'll be rewarded with lore reveals and a general better understanding of the game.

The movement is... not the greatest aspect of this game. It's pretty clunky, and a lot of the times it feels like your inputs simply aren't registered correctly, which may lead to deaths that could have easily been prevented by smoother movement.

Overall, this game is amazing. It is a masterclass of worldbuilding, smart enemies, visual storytelling, exploration, and more. I highly recommend that you at least give this game a try, and maybe by one of the DLCs while you're at it.

This game is astonishing. Not perfect, mind you, but I think it could be said that this game sets a standard for what more games should strive to be- an art piece expressed through an interactive experience. I believe a lot of this game's imperfections are based in the mechanical game experience, as a byproduct of this goal. However, let me first explain where this approach went very VERY right.

This game is best known for its immersive world, most notably its AI. Every creature in a region exists independently from the player and has its own agency. This was the intent of the devs, and I think they achieved this goal with immense success. Even when offscreen, mock simulations are done between hundreds of different creatures and often you will run into scenes where the ecosystem is acting naturally. This approach to immersive world design is incredibly effective at making your character seem more at odds with the world and aids in the overarching plot in that sense. It also means you can use these immersive behaviors to your advantage, depending on how things are layed out at the start of a cycle.

The various creatures of the world are rendered procedurally, drawn over a skeleton that is used for physics simulation and behavior. This also helps to make these creatures seem more lively. Only a few creatures notably have any proper means of expression, but by the way creatures seem to move or behave the intent and emotion of each creature is supposed by the player. Removing the limitation of frame by frame handiwork animation allows for the player to insert their own characters into the creatures they encounter.

The world is very interactive and alive, and that is this game's primary goal and where it strives the most.

I do also generally love how the game feels as an experience, although this is where I have to break down a few caveats. This is a review, after all, and I feel there are some aspects of this game that can be a deterrent to some types of player. A lot of these "imperfections," however, are a matter of perspective. You may enjoy the effect that these factors have on the game, or you may loathe them. That's why I felt they deserved so much discussion here.

Due to the agency lent to creatures in the open world, there is a tendency for variance in difficulty. By circumstance, all the lizards in a region could have found their way into the same room and you could be forced to fight through or go around. While variance is usually a welcome surprise, sometimes this could mean attempting a section hundreds of times over.

At which point it's worth mentioning, death is not inconsequential in this game. Every cycle you survive grants you a level of Karma, which decreases with each death. I commend their attempts to make this system work, however: karma is not a conventional "lives" system, no. Rather it works as a key to various gates between regions, requiring you to have a minimum karma to pass through. This enables them to require the player to learn a region before progressing, or perhaps reward good play with gates that access harder but faster regions. I never personally had any run-ins with karma being difficult to attain at a gate, but this game is a challenge and it is a worthy deterrent.

Hibernating during a cycle not only increases karma, but it moves some creatures around. This is a useful tool, but it's worth noting that this is also your save system. You *must* be able to survive long enough to find food or you will not be able to save progress. Leaving a game 30 seconds into a cycle WILL affect karma and count as a loss.
Every cycle saves the current position of things before you leave your saferoom. This can compound on the first point; not only can rooms be difficult by chance, you can be forced to encounter these rooms until you can save again. Optimistically, this means teaching the player how to handle themselves in these random encounters and giving them the chance to learn how to approach these situations each cycle, but again... this is a matter of perspective.

Lastly, this game DOES require a guide. As immersive as it is, it is also expansive and does not hold hands. There is an ingame guide creature that follows you around, but he disappears occasionally and is usually quite vague beyond pointing to hazards and food sources. I do not recommend using a guide for the first few regions, though- the process of learning creatures and their habits is a large portion of the experience.
I recommend pulling up maps and asking for directions to progress, and even then only at around the point you get to the Shoreline region. Avoid creature guides unless you require them, however there are a few things that are poorly communicated that may end up being necessary in some points of progression.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game, but I can acknowledge that a handful of people may find it frustrating or generally not be inclined to play their money's worth out of it. For all that this game aims to be, though, I think it is critically amazing.

[EDIT] Forgot to include a couple of actually genuine criticisms:
1. enemies are completely capable of sitting at the entrance of the other side of a pipe. This WILL happen a handful of times, where first time through a cycle you will die without any hope of reacting to these moments.
2. no camera control at all, which would be fine if the camera wasn't always fixed somewhere. Some rooms are multiple screens in size, and often times the camera will refuse to adjust to the next half of it until you're already offscreen. This becomes a problem when you're in a room with platforming or enemies, so it definitely will occur a handful of times as well. MOST rooms avoid this issue, though, and aren't too large.

In my experience, this game is very difficult to stick with. Once you push through that initial frustration in those first 10 or so hours however, this game becomes one of the most rewarding video game experiences in the medium both in mechanics and narrative. I strongly suggest going in completely blind, and explore at your own pace, as there are many experiences that this game offers that I will remember for many years to come.

This game isn’t bad; I’m just disappointed that I don’t like it. My first three hours were apprehensive and exciting unlike anything I've ever played before, and I love games that withhold context and force the player to deeply think. But it quickly deteriorated into mundanity for three main reasons: the visuals and sounds of most areas are homogeneous (never mind that the music didn't often function properly), threats quickly became nonthreatening since most are introduced in the first few areas, and the vaguely telegraphed objectives had me discover almost the entire map across ~50 hours before I advanced the story even once. I think these are all legitimate justifications for my frustration, and even if my 76-hour playthrough is abnormally long for one playthrough, this could've easily been avoided because I don't actually think any of these problems were mistakes. Despite my frustration, I always suspected that this game was special, and I'm happy that I had the patience to discover a few key sequences in this game that commanded my attention more than nearly anything I've ever seen. The soundtrack, graphics (that are somehow merely pixel art), style, and presentation are near-perfect. It's also refreshing to see the game succeed at the authentic Lovecraftian approach (not the lazy 'giant flesh blob with lots of teeth' approach that most people think is Lovecraftian) by fully admitting that it can't represent the divine, the afterlife, or infinity. I genuinely mean all of that, yet in doing some research, I realized that this game wasn't designed around any of it (and therefore players like me). Nearly everything I dislike about this game was a choice, not a lack of skill. It was designed to be an intentionally difficult (and sometimes unfair) ecological simulation, and I think it does this exceedingly well. I can only fairly say that I'm disappointed that an incredibly rich world is communicated mostly through intentionally unfair gameplay. This excessively shrouds the story in mystery for its own sake, and isn't conducive for facilitating an emotional connection with it, but a few key moments still make Rain World one of the most beautiful games I've ever seen, and it's very obvious to me why it's so loved.

Fantastic game without equal in it's space. Extremely well-thought-out deeper lore, and AI systems to the point they would be worthy of an early college-level game design class to study, culminating in a perfectly living world in relation to the player. Problems with movement can be solved by mods to the point it becomes a tight and well-polished but natural-feeling platformer that feels very satisfying just to to move around in.
There is simply nothing like it.
BUT... it is underrated for good reason, beginning utterly directionless and devoid of motivation or clear cause, and with points that go beyond the intended sense of unfairness into utter monotony retrying the same things over and over. For example, one of my favorite segments involved avoiding the particularly *clanky* creature by running through pipes between waves, but after failing just near the end a few times, it suddenly wasn't worth running through the part I knew I could now easily complete (albeit quite slowly), and to save the extended hassle i downloaded a mod to delete my very favorite creature from the game, and another that allowed increased game speed. 
One of my favorite levels became a simple waste of time.
I have a hobby of editing videos for Youtube, and as I get better I see more and more clearly the points where these things would lose people—where disengagement would spike—and the entire first half (or more if you try to go left for any reason before meeting a few friends [like me]) is the biggest killer of interest I can imagine, to the point I have no idea how it was left this way by release. Upon replaying the first half, the editor in me screams CUT CUT CUT at every possible interval because the pacing is just... Bad. The little yellow doodle that tells you where to go barely ever... actually tells you... where to go? There are many areas that are either pointless or near-impassible without knowledge you can only really gain by... passing through those areas? I truly believe this game would've soared to popularity if the main difficulty of the game was the gameplay, and not finding the will to keep boggling around every little nook and cranny you haven't gone down just trying to find the way to the story. In my opinion, all they had to do was make that yellow noodle just a little less like a buffoon, and a little more like The Stanley Parable Adventure Line™.

I am among only 8% of people that ever beat the game after buying it.

My advice? Buy the game without a second thought, but unless you like mind-numbing suffering, get someone with a corporeal form to give you those subtle hints on where to go next. That is, until you get to the fantastic second half, where every way you go is different way forward, before, finally, someone who isn't stupid tells you the *real* way out.

I want to love this game so goddamn much. Its world is evocative and I love its feel, but I just 
can't stand how stupidly punishing the world is. For the record, I love hard games, Dark Souls and Hollow Knight are some of my favorites. The difference is that in those games, you can learn from your mistakes. When you get hit in Dark Souls, you know why and can avoid it the next time. Rain World is just obtuse and random. I think the straw that broke me was when I was traversing some pipes. There is a drowning system in the game, but the game gives you no indication (that I can see) as to how close you are to dying instantly from drowning. So, after dying over and over again from drowning in these pipes, I finally made it through the area. I went through a pipe, and on the other side was a massive vulture creature. I was dead in seconds, and had to go through the entire area again, only to make it a few more feet forward before THREE vultures killed me. 

Also, fuck any area in this game with leechs in water that you have to swim through.

I think this game is so obtuse because it wants you to learn through trial and error, but death in this game is brutal. Resting is expensive, and areas are gated behind multiple rests that you cannot die inbetween.

I think half the issue I have in this game is a result of the frustration from Karma Gates. I loved Hollow Knight because I would just stumble into a whole new massive area by accident. You can fall into one of the hardest areas of the game by accident. You can't do that in Rain World, and every death means another 10 minutes before you can explore a new area, and death is almost always instant and unavoidable. There were multiple times where I was stuck with 3 lizards who can one shot me on both sides of a pipe, and I'd just have to spam back and forth hoping they would somehow let me through. 

The areas in this game are massive, but they aren't *interesting*. There's so many screens that are just tiled version of the area, with no purpose. Again, I hate to keep bringing up Hollow Knight, but I think that game is what this game should've been like. Most rooms in Hollow Knight are designed carefully, and its areas are smaller but more dense. 

I also wish this game had upgrades. I never felt like I was actually progressing, just moving to different areas. I never wanted to explore because there was almost nothing to find except gates to other vast, empty areas. I think the random enemy generation is the problem here, no encounter is actually designed, leading to shitty random swarms of 4 vultures and unavoidable death.

I'm going to watch a Lets Play of this, because I want to see more of this world, but I just wish the developers wanted me to see it.

[h1]This game is absolutely amazing. But recommending it is kind of tricky.[/h1]
Let me be clear. This game is hard. It is so incredibly difficult, not to mention the somewhat lacking tutorial or number of apparent things you need to know but are never told. This game will kill you a thousand times. It will make you suffer. Many times you will think you have died unfairly and maybe you will even be right.
However, what I find amazing is that this is sort of meant to be a part of the experience. Keep in mind, this is not a game you're supposed to get good at. This is not a game in which you will find amazing gear or learn special tricks and will suddenly shred your enemies. In this game, you are both a predator and a prey. But you are a prey more than you are a predator. You are like a rabbit running away from wolves and foxes. And rabbits never get good at killing foxes.
So don't expect to play this game and at one point run through danger like it's nothing. You will always only be a Slugcat in a world where most of the things are far more dangerous than you are. You will however get better at detecting threats before they happen, you will get better at running away and staying away from danger, you will figure out how to kill predators in some situations if situation demands and allows you to.
Granted, punishment for death is not too big, but it's still frustrating.

This all said, the game is absolutely beautiful. It has amazing emotional music filled with ideas you may not notice immediately. It's easy to get lost in music because it so often just perfectly fits the kind of area you are in. It's difficult to put to words just how well this is done.
Atmosphere in this game is also fantastically well made. Everything from colors, to details, to random growth of plants at places. You can almost feel the overarching emotion emanating from certain places. That mixed with music and this game becomes quite a unique experience.
And the world building. Going through the ruins of an ancient civilization and learning piece by piece of what that world was like and what has happened. Lore of this game is vast. Playing for the first time you will be confused, but also intrigued. How the world looks like, how it feels, how it interacts with itself and with you.
The way creatures behave for example. Just how lifelike they are. How they ambush, chase, utilize their biology to their advantage. How they run away from other creatures which are bigger than them, how they respond to sound or sight. How they chase their prey be it Slugcat or not. They are done better than in almost any other game. They truly feel alive and feel like part of the world. As with everything in this game, they are not here just to be obstacles. They are here because they live here.

In terms of plot, [spoiler]it's strange. End of the game is open to interpretation, though if you spend time learning about game lore, you are sure to understand it. No one tells you what you did, why or how it relates to various images or dreams you've had. You just do it and then ask yourself what that was.[/spoiler]

Point is, playing this game, you will feel an overwhelming sense of wonder, beauty, amazement, and probably feel like crying on few occasions whether from emotional elements of the game, or just from dying too many times. Rainworld definitely requires a special kind of mindset to fully enjoy. This game gave me PTSD and then proceeded to cure it with it's beauty and wonder. The experience is unlike any other.
If dying and frustration bothers you, this game will feel like 7.5/10.
If you can get past the dying and frustration, you will enjoy 9.5/10 experience.
To me, this is truly one of the best games ever made. Words can't do it justice. It's definitely worth the money, but I don't think it's for everyone.

[h1]Full Review[/h1]
I found this game through my wife’s obsession with its lore. I tried it out and quickly became frustrated with its difficulty, but it sat at the back of my mind until I played again. I still got frustrated, but I was doing better. And still I repeated this process. Now, 100+ hours in, the game still manages to annoy me sometimes…and yet there’s nothing quite like the feeling of curiosity and adventure it gives. That’s what keeps bringing me back to Rain World.

Gameplay:
Rain World has a high learning curve. You are tossed into the game after a brief cutscene, taught the basic mechanics of controls, eating food to survive, and finding shelter from the titular rain before the end of each cycle. After that, there’s next to no instruction, and you’re left to wander around and figure everything else out yourself.
One of the most curious features in Rain World that you’ll quickly notice is the other nonplayer creatures. Rather than being traditional video game enemies and whatnot, they behave more like animals in an environment simulation, traveling around the region and doing things on their own accord. Some are passive toward you, while others become aggressive and need to be foiled in order for you to survive.
Which leads to another key point: your character is small, weak, and delicious, and your abilities are limited. Besides the low-damage spears you can find scattered around, there’s very few consistent methods to fight back against dangerous creatures. As such, you instead must learn how to outsmart, outplay, and outmaneuver anything that wants to eat or kill you. Along with survival, platforming skills and devious wit become imperative for progression. This is where a lot of the unfairness comes into play, as during some cycles it will just feel like everything is working against you. It can work the opposite way as well, however, as random situations or thinking outside the box can lead to unexpected solutions for moving forward. Such a fascinatingly random environment is both this game’s biggest annoyance, and greatest reward.

Story:
Rather than a traditional linear story, Rain World is more of an anthology of its own ingame world, told through the small and comparatively insignificant struggles of each character’s campaign. Even then, little of that lore is given to you directly, but rather must be gleaned from piecing together environmental clues or dialogue from ancient beings. This form of storytelling fits well with the game, making you once again feel like just a small critter in a world that lives on, with or without you. Those who can figure out Rain World’s lore will find it unique and fascinating. Don’t worry, I won’t spoil any of it!

Visuals:
This is another section where Rain World stands out from other games. The graphics are clearly pixelated yet highly detailed, playing well to the visual storytelling I mentioned earlier. Each creature, including yourself, is actually procedurally-animated, causing them to move even more lifelike…usually. Sometimes the procedural animation can glitch and create some humorous results, haha. Even still, the graphics and procedural animation in particular are often a wonderous sight to behold.

Music:
I’m normally not good at saying much for this section but holy hecc does Rain World leave an impression here. The soundtrack is absolutely a perfect match for this game. Much of the music almost feels diegetic as you explore, and the dynamic threat music for whenever danger is nearby fits the riskiness of each encounter.
But what sticks out in particular to me is the main theme. Along with the title screen version, it plays in three other variants throughout your adventure. It’s such a simple tune, yet the more I’ve learned about Rain World’s lore, the more I feel it perfectly encapsulates the game world’s themes and condition. It is hauntingly beautiful, and almost nostalgic in a way. Very few soundtracks can get me emotional in the same way.

Replay Value:
Although the game’s world stays the same for each given campaign, the high randomness factor and generally nonlinear exploration make Rain World a great game to play over and over. Many secrets lay hidden throughout each campaign, and even without, there’s plenty of fun to be had in challenging yourself to different completion methods or scores.

In conclusion, Rain World is a highly unique exploration game experience that is really worth a look. Thanks to its high learning curve, this game unfortunately might not be for everyone, especially if you get frustrated easily. But those who are looking to try something new, and are willing to use a bit of patience, will find this game unforgettable.

A lot of people will criticise this game for several reasons. Allow me to summarise them and spare you the time spent scrolling through identical negative reviews.

Here's what people don't like:

1. The controls are imprecise 
2. The enemies are unpredictable
3. The ending is weird
4. The difficulty is too high

Can I disagree with these? Not at all! Rain World is a hard game. It will frustrate you. Several times I have had to stop myself from injuring my laptop after my 43rd bullshit death against the blue octopus things that hang around the zero-gravity area. I have angrily quit this game at least 7 times. Does this mean it's a bad game? Of course not.

The game is hard. But don't you remember when all games were as hard, if not harder than this? When did we collectively decide that hard=bad? I understand the concerns, though. Rain World is not hard in the same way that Super Meat Boy is hard. The difficulty comes from factors you often can't control. Enemy placement, unclear platforms, unreliability of food spawns, all contriubte to the difficulty. It's tough, I won't understate that, and often not for the right reasons.

However, I keep coming back. Do you know why?

It's because frustration from continually missing that fucking jump fades. What remains is the sense of wonder and awe at the beauty of the environments, the immersiveness of the world, and the absolutely stunning visual design. Simply looking at this game is absolutely entrancing, and finding new and varied environments is very rewarding. People complain about the ending- That's a personal issue. I thought the ending, and the lore surrounding it that you can organically work out was a very interesting conclusion. It leaves questions, but, to anyone familiar with the game; Wouldn't it be a bit underwhelming if you just found this super secret area with all your family there, reuinted with them, and then ended the game?

The world sets up something much bigger than that. The architecture of the levels is clearly intentional, clearly alluding to a fallen civilisation- one you are able to find out. The world of this game is bigger than you, bigger than your family, and the ending creates a very enthralling conclusion to that, giving a hint into what became of the world at large.

Essentially, exploring the world and finding out the lore is fun and rewarding, if sometimes frustrating. I would highly recommend this game. Give it some time, give it some effort. You will be rewarded.

There are very few games that I can say with certainty manage to accomplish the feats that Rain World achieves. This game and its developers were focused on one sole goal when creating this game, to create a living world.
This one goal permeates through the entire being of Rain World so heavily, to the point that it becomes the source of all the criticisms and all the praise that Rain World garners.

 There are many sacrifices that the developers had to make in order to ensure this living world was as realistic as possible, and many of you might find these features rage-inducing to the level of dropping this game entirely. So let me reiterate, THIS GAME MAKES NO COMPROMISES. It will never meet the player half-way, it will never bend its rules to assist the player, the game and its world is truly and utterly indifferent whether you live or die. You can play Rain World perfectly and still fail.

So despite all this, why do I recommend this game? Why it is in my top 5 of all time?  Because for the more patient of players, the ones who are stubborn and refuse to get discouraged by the brutality that Rain World forces upon you at every turn, you will find the beauty in Rain World. That uncompromising mindset I mentioned earlier is the reason Rain World is second to none in immersion, world building and moment to moment game play. The living aspect of this world allows for some of the most frustrating, keyboard smashing low points, as well as the most adrenaline-pumping, heart-stopping high points. And when this game is at its best, you find yourself in awe at its beauty, enraptured by its sound track and laughing as you plunge into the crazy fray of monsters duking it out in front of you because there is shelter just behind them and the rain is coming soon..

Do yourself a favor, when you get frustrated with this game,  step away, take a moment and come back another day. Because when you come back, Rain World will be waiting with a brand new experience and new creative ways to kill you.

You'll see a lot of reviews about how Rain World is difficult but yet VERY worth it, or how Rain World isn't a baby's game for baby people or whatever. Personally, I find that the "git gud" mentality doesn't work very well in Rain World. Let me explain.

If you've played Celeste, you'll know that you'll die hundreds if not thousands of times and the game is rather proud to declare that at the end of its technically demanding platforming sections. You die instantly in Celeste, like most platformers. You die instantly in Rain World too, but this is a survival platformer. You'll have to crawl your mangy hide all the way back to where you had just painstakingly gotten to and pray you can get yourself from Point A to B in that room safely.

Is it frustrating? Absolutely! Probably everyone in this review section has a story of a particularly huge defeat and they just... don't play Rain World for a week, month or two. **Rain World is not everyone's cup of tea.**

But if you're certain that you're determined to learn more about Why you insta-died to this one enemy, or How you can out-run a flying monster, or Where the most reliable food sources are... you'll find that Rain World has an incredibly engrossing story, cosmology, genuinely intelligent AI, and beautiful art and animation. It's seriously a gem.

But it's pretty damn hard to see if a diamond's worth it when it's uncut. You'll need to take the plunge to find out. Good luck, and I hope you enjoyed it as much as I do. Don't get upset when you die - it never mattered in the first place. ;-)

When you start out nothing makes sense and you will die often, when you die you will lose a symbol that you don't understand what it means, this may make you upset but don't let it, if you don't know what the symbol is for then what does losing one matter? As you progress you will learn how to play, not through a forced tutorial or someone telling you but by experiencing it yourself, you discover the many moves Slugcat has (Far more than the basic movement and jump the game does tell you about), you will start to understand why you rolled instead of doing what you wanted to and then you will learn how to control the game correctly and it will feel lke a breath of fresh air.
