Don't be fooled by the tags: Rain World does not make for much of a platformer. However, that doesn't mean it's not well worth playing. If you're looking for a game that's challenging, features a significant learning curve, and offers a large world to explore, then Rain World may be worth your consideration. Just maybe approach it as more of an exploration-oriented survival game.

Now, I really do love this game a lot. The playtime listed above should be proof of that. However, I'd be remiss not to warn you of what to expect going in.

One characteristic feature of the game is that Slugcat requires much more active and hands-on control than many players will be used to. The game only teaches you the bare minimum needed to get around; and in the hands of a novice, Slugcat will be very clumsy. Much of your adventure will be spent learning how to get around and, bit by bit, just how much you're really capable of. There are no levels or being taught new skills. Instead, learning something new usually comes down to doing it by mistake, and following through on it to try and figure out how you did it, and how to do it consistently. In that way, the learning process feels very organic—and there's a crowd out there that will very much appreciate that. For others, it will make Rain World a difficult game to approach.

The world can also be an unforgiving, cruel place. Slugcat is stuck in the middle of the food chain, and the game does a great job making sure you know that. Learning to avoid becoming someone's lunch is par for the course, but there are absolutely some areas of the game which require extra persistence and care to navigate through safely. While there is almost always a way around, getting out of a tough spot sometimes require mastery in its own right.

Now, beyond (but also encompassing) the game being difficult, the AI is excellent with regards to what the game has set out to do, in that characteristically difficult-to-learn way. Rain World features a colourful and diverse cast of creatures, each suitably adapted to the areas they're found in. And while what each creature is capable of is consistent, it can be difficult to gauge the motivation of each individual you encounter. Are those bugs going to be friendly, and how far is that lizard willing to chase you? As you explore to new, more exotic places, the game will also have new creatures to introduce to you. In another case of the game doing what it does [i]very[/i] well, you'll never be quite sure how to approach them at first. Rain World had me second-guessing how to approach each new creature right up until the end.

And as implied, the game offers a variety of ecosystems to explore, each with a unique blend of features, landscapes, and native fauna. Every area offers different challenges when it comes to navigating and avoiding enemies within them, even without the fundamentals changing at all. Each area is a little different—sometimes [i]very[/i] different—from the one that came before, and each winds up being memorable. The many areas of Rain World also connect to each other in a loose network, meaning there's many ways to cross from one part of the world to another.

Now, I know a lot of what I've discussed sums up to "The game is hard." It is! But it's able to offer a lot of fun (to some) for a very long time. There's a lot to explore; and the independent, sometimes fickle creatures keep things fresh. There's also a lot of interesting hidden mechanics that take time to tease out; and mastering new movement always, [i]always[/i] feels satisfying. I even enjoyed wracking my brain on how to navigate around dangerous creatures in the most difficult areas of the game (and those areas remain some of my favourites).

[b]Rain World is absolutely not a game I would recommend indiscriminately.[/b] If the fundamental challenge of learning how to get around, or the anxiety of being pursued by a hungry predator, or the possibility of getting stuck somewhere because the area is difficult are making you feel iffy about buying Rain World, then I'd recommend passing on it or enjoying it vicariously through a streamer a little more familiar with it. However, if everything it has to offer sounds interesting to you, [i]then yes, I wholeheartedly recommend it[/i]. It was a very satisfying experience for me, and I know it will be for many others. I just don't want people to go in expecting something other than what they're going to get.

As an aside, the game [i]has[/i] become more approachable since I first played it, with the addition of the Monk: a Slugcat who encounters fewer, less aggressive creatures, and requires less food. But if a challenging experience is absolutely what you're looking for, then the Survivor is still an excellent choice and my personal recommendation for the most authentic experience.

[h1] Rain World is an absolutely exceptional game I'm not afraid to call the masterpiece of modern game industry.[/h1]
Rain World is a well crafted combination of gameplay mechanics, philosophical ideas and charming aesthetics. This creation is unfair and absolutely is a niche game. [list]
[*] [b]The world that feels alive.[/b] Getting chased by a Lizard while running under a random Dropwig waiting for pray making it jump on you but actually attacking The Lizard and making them lose interest in you while they fight for their lives. Do you think this is a rare situation in this game? Not at all. Rain World ecosphere feels as alive as it can get and physics based environment emphasizes this very well. Creatures hunt, fight, fool around and survive the same as you. AI in this game is simply amazing and even simply observing it is fun.

[*] [b]The OST.[/b] The Survivor intro music still makes me cry every time I listen to it. The "Urban Jungle" when you enter Outskirts? "Moondown" giving you a feel of shared loneliness with a character while telling you "not so alone now you two" while giving new hope. When "Lantern Mice" plays in the Shaded Citadel. "Stargazer" after you exit The Exterior and see the ruins of the past civilizations feeling so alone, but now you have an end destination in your story. "Raindeer Ride" when you're traveling in almost no comeback region of the game knowing that your fate is almost sealed and this is your last moments on the surface. I don't want to spoil all of it. OST of this game is another topic and it absolutely nails the point of the game. It's simply beautiful, charming and emotional, while being unique and pretty diverse.

[*][b]Learning curve and difficulty.[/b] While at first you feel like a small creature testing its limits and trying to survive as best as it can the more experienced and smart you become the more connected to the slugcat you become. Learning to use stuff versus predators, learning to hunt, learning advanced movement and how creatures and the world behave: all of this feels really rewarding. The game itself is really hard, especially in the beginning and even after 100+ hours into the game I still can get mad when I'm getting really unlucky, but for me this is the part of the experience: this game is unfair. The world is unfair. Deal with it. Be smart and skillful and survive no matter the odds or be the prey. All I can advice is that you need to be patient with your few hours in this game. I would say that after 15-20 hours into the game a really small percentage of players feel the same type of frustration they feel at first. Even if you're angry at this point there's no turning back from the charm of this game. I myself almost dropped the game after first 5 hours, but I decided to comeback and be more patient.

[*][b]Aesthetic and atmosphere.[/b] The game perfectly combines sci-fi, post-apocalyptic and buddhist themes. Aesthetic and the atmosphere of this game are really unique and feel like nothing I tried before. Rain World feels like a combination of Dark Souls and Silent Hill to me. Apathy, both hope and hopelessness, loneliness, fear, decay, anger. This game makes you feel such an array of different emotions and feelings. It is absolutely indescribable.

[*][b]Point of the game.[/b] When I first started playing this game I was desperate for a route, for answers, for anything. I did not agree with the rain cycles mechanic, neither did I like some other game mechanics. My first hours into the game felt pretty negative and I somewhat hollow. I didn't know what I should do, but the more I played and the more experienced I become as a slugcat the more I saw the point of this game: there's no point. You can do whatever you want: survive, tame predators, kill dangerous creatures, explore, learn, kill for no reason or try to follow the storyline for each slugcat. You're free to do whatever you want. There's is a road you can take that will take you to the "end" of this game as fast as possible, but there's absolutely no need in doing this. Rain World is not a story based game that is needed to be finished as fast as possible. The ending will probably will leave you with a feeling of emptiness and demanding for answers. The moment I started taking big steps, learning how to survive, how to live and thrive and do whatever I wanted - it was the moment I knew I love this game. Everything else was just a bonus, things I can do, a route I can take, a journey I might go on, but everything is optional. I don't think I completed the game first time until at least 60~ hours into the game. And to be fair you can complete the story of the game in 2-3~ hours as a new player if you really want to. Do whatever you want and you will not regret it.

[*][b]Lore.[/b] I will not go in-depth for this one, the game lore is hard to connect and find. You can complete the game without understanding anything, but the lore itself is pretty interesting. You will rarely have a full picture of what's going in this world, but when you connect the pieces - it will feel like you're archaeologist dug up a picture of the past that makes sense why everything that is happening now the way it is. A lot of mysteries, vague concepts combined with logical and scientific stuff. The lore of this game is pretty interesting.
   [/list]

[b] Here are some moments I still see as mistakes, bad game design choices or simply annoying, some of them are subjective, but some need real fixing: [/b]

[list]
[*] Rain World is a game about exploration and experimentation, yet the game has a tendency to punish you for it at times. Feels like a conflict in game design of Rain World. Wasn't a major issue for me after 15~ hours into the game though.

[*] In most games I tend to ignore tutorials, but Rain World really needs one. There's no way you're going to learn all about the movement and stuff like Spore Puffs and why they're needed without using the wiki.

[*] Rain World rarely rewards you for combat. This is somewhat fixed by the Hunter slugcat, but outside of Vulture masks I see little need in combat as a Survivor slugcat.

[*] Scavengers need fixing. They will kill you on accident trying to kill Overseers no matter how high your reputation is, while they obviously care about each other and wont do the same to their own kind. They will teleport into Shelters while following you even after the door has closed stealing all of your stuff and blocking you for a good minute in there in the next cycle. Maddening.

[*] In some places you jump down a pit and there's a platform, in some places it's a deathpit. In some places you climb up a wall to get into the next room, but there's an invisible "rubber wall" forcing you back. Sometimes this stuff is just not as obvious as you want it to be.
[/list]

Summing up my review all I can say in the end is that Rain World is definitely a special game that I truly consider a piece of art. It is one of the most important games of my life and I would advise anyone to at least give it a good try. [b]Videocult[/b], thank you for such a masterpiece.

It's very much its own simulated world, with intricately designed mechanics that don't inherently relate to the player nor the gameplay. All the other animals act much like you, hunting, scavenging, and exploring. It's an extremely immersive game with a lot of moving pieces, even when you're not looking.

It took me several hours playing this game to finally not suck at the controls (and I still don't like them) and MANY more hours to get combat down (and after that, I downloaded several mods that improve the controls, however non-vanilla they may be.) 

Half the time the game doesn't want you to progress. Get to a new zone, die several times due to bad luck or short cycle time, which will deter you a lot when playing the game. In fact, there's more times when I get frustrated than I do enjoy myself, at a 60/40 margin (pulling that out of my ass lol).

But when the game does work, when you finally get a comeback, kill that lizard, or make it to the next gate or shelter, it's a joyride.

Even though I've been dismayed more times than simply enjoying the game, when I DO enjoy the game, It's an indescribable experience - like watching a piece of art get an extended foot of canvas, or an immense wave of relief of overcoming a difficult or albeit tedious challenge.

I think there's definitely a way to make this game better, without sacrificing the core mechanics or difficulty, but I think there's a hard layer of reddit-hive-mind people that defend this game without a doubt in their mind, and may be the reason or are at least contributing to the absolute zero change in how the game works from the devs part (with the steam workshop it's not entirely necessary, but there are going to be a lot of people who try this game pure vanilla, and will hate it like I did at first). 

I think these people have experienced the same level of tedium that I have with this game, which it isn't too horrible, but it's definitely enough to look at this game objectively and say it's extremely flawed. A good amount of the time the game doesn't really play like an actual video game, and that can be incredibly frustrating when you're just trying to progress.

If the developers ever get the idea of making a sequel to this game (somehow), I'd really think it'd be neat to see a more refined and non-obtuse form of game that's still similar to the first one, and this time actually developed with the idea of making a game in mind rather than just a concrete jungle simulator.

besides all of that, this game is incredibly good. I may sound harsh on it but that's just because it's an old game that still gets recent updates and dlc - but I just really want people to enjoy this game to its fullest and also remind those that might pick this game up - don't feel any guilt with trying mods. Vanilla purism isn't really all that, and there's no shame in playing the game how you want. With that said, I still recommend trying rain world at least once!
